idea: Replace the random shuffle with a target-similarity filter. In select(): (1) drop exact duplicates by hashing the stripped text; (2) drop docs whose alphabetic-character fraction is below 0.7, or that look like spam (e.g. contain "Click here", "coupon", "discount code", "free shipping"); (3) fit sklearn TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2, stop_words="english") on target_sample plus the surviving docs, and score each doc by cosine similarity to the mean target_sample vector; (4) sort docs by score descending, with ties broken by the seeded RNG from CURATE_SEED; (5) walk the sorted list, accumulating an approximate token count (len(text)/4 per doc), and stop once it reaches T, so the returned list covers about T tokens with no cycling needed. Use the same seeded order as the fallback if fewer than T tokens survive.
why: The target domain is Wikipedia-style encyclopedic articles, while the pool is about half off-domain noise (spam, forum posts, news, junk), so keeping only clean, deduplicated, target-similar documents should put more in-domain tokens into the fixed 9.83M-token budget and lower held-out bpb relative to the random-order baseline.
outcome: dev 1.9533 against 1.9583 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the seeded random shuffle as the final order, but first remove near-duplicates and junk. (a) Drop docs whose alphabetic-character fraction is below 0.7 or that contain spam phrases ("Click here", "coupon", "discount code", "free shipping", "order ... online"). (b) Near-duplicate removal: build word 5-gram shingle sets per doc, compute MinHash with 64 seeded hash permutations, use LSH banding (16 bands of 4 rows) to find candidate pairs, and keep a doc only if its estimated Jaccard with every already-kept doc is below 0.5. Process candidates in the seeded shuffle order so the kept doc is random. (c) Return the shuffled survivors; if they total fewer than T tokens, cycle them as the trainer already does. Do not use target similarity or truncate to T tokens.
why: The pool has many templated spam and repeated boilerplate documents, so near-duplicate removal should raise the share of distinct natural text inside the first T tokens without narrowing the domain the way the rejected similarity-cutoff filter did.
outcome: dev 1.9960 against 1.9583 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), replace the cosine-to-mean-centroid score with a domain classifier score, and drop the alphabetic-fraction and spam-phrase rules. Fit sklearn TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2, stop_words="english") on target_sample plus all docs. Train LogisticRegression(C=1.0, class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000) with the 200 target_sample docs as positives and a seeded random sample of 200 pool docs as negatives. Score every pool doc with predict_proba for the positive class; for pool docs that were sampled as negatives, use 5-fold cross-fitted predictions so they are not scored by a model that saw them. Order docs by score descending, breaking ties with random.Random(int(os.environ.get("CURATE_SEED", 0))). Exact-duplicate removal by hashing the stripped text stays. Walk the sorted list, accumulating len(text)/4 per doc, and stop once the total reaches T, as in experiment 1. Use the seeded shuffle as the fallback if fewer than T tokens survive.
why: Experiment 1 showed that ranking by target similarity helps a little (1.9533 vs 1.9583), while experiment 2's hard junk and alphabetic-fraction rules hurt badly (1.996), probably because they removed useful Wikipedia-style text containing " @-@ " and numbers; a learned domain classifier should rank by target-likeness without those brittle hand-written cutoffs.
outcome: dev 1.9847 against 1.9583 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the baseline seeded random shuffle as the final order, but drop only damaged/scrambled docs using a vocabulary-coverage test instead of the alphabetic-fraction rule. In select(): (1) exact-dedupe by hashing the stripped text (as in experiment 1). (2) Build a vocabulary set = lowercased alphabetic words that appear in target_sample, plus words whose document frequency across the pool is at least 20. (3) For each doc, compute the fraction of its alphabetic word tokens (lowercased, regex [A-Za-z]+) that are in the vocabulary; drop the doc if the fraction is below 0.6 or it has fewer than 5 words. Do not apply the alpha-fraction threshold or spam-phrase rules. (4) Return the seeded shuffle of the survivors, with no truncation, so the trainer reads them front to back and cycles only if needed.
why: Experiment 2 likely hurt because its alphabetic-fraction rule discarded legitimate wiki-style text (with " @-@ " and numbers), so a damage detector based on whether words are real English words, calibrated on target vocabulary, should remove the scrambled docs without losing target-domain text.
outcome: dev 1.9470 against 1.9583 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Keep the current best pipeline (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter, seeded shuffle, no truncation) and add a format-match filter. For each doc, compute its "wiki-style token ratio": the fraction of whitespace-separated tokens that are standalone punctuation or markers (e.g. ",", ".", "(", ")", ";", ":", "@-@", "@.@", "@,@", "=" headers). Compute the median of this ratio over target_sample, and drop any pool doc whose ratio is below 0.5 times that median. Leave the vocabulary-coverage rule and the seeded shuffle order unchanged, and do not truncate.
why: The target and the best-kept pool docs use the WikiText-style spaced-punctuation and "@-@" tokenization, while many surviving pool docs are web or forum text with normal spacing whose words still pass the vocabulary-coverage test, so a structural format filter should remove them and keep the training distribution closer to the target.
outcome: dev 1.9931 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the current best pipeline unchanged (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter, seeded shuffle, no truncation) but raise the coverage threshold from _MIN_COVERAGE = 0.6 to 0.75 and add a fallback: compute the total len(text)/4 token estimate of the survivors, and if it is below T, relax the threshold back to 0.6 (and, if still short, keep the 0.6 survivors and shuffle as now). Leave _MIN_DF = 20, _MIN_WORDS = 5, the vocabulary construction and the seeded shuffle exactly as they are.
why: Training only reads about T of the roughly 2T-token pool, so a stricter damage filter costs no usable data as long as survivors still cover T tokens, and the fallback prevents cycling; this is an untested threshold sweep on the one rule that has actually helped (the 0.6 coverage filter took dev from 1.9583 to 1.9470).
outcome: dev 1.9568 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the current best pipeline (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter at _MIN_COVERAGE=0.6, _MIN_DF=20, _MIN_WORDS=5, no truncation), but replace the uniform seeded shuffle in step (4) with a quality-ordered list. Compute each survivor's coverage fraction (share of its [A-Za-z]+ lowercased words in vocab). First apply the seeded shuffle to the survivors as before, then run a stable sort by coverage descending (Python's sort is stable, so the seeded order breaks ties). Return that order with no truncation, so the trainer still cycles only if needed. The filter set and the tokens are unchanged; only the order differs.
why: The pool holds about 2T tokens and training stops after T, so roughly the first half of the returned order is what gets read, which means the order decides which documents are used; putting the cleanest, most in-vocabulary documents first should lower bpb, and unlike the rejected similarity-sort and truncation experiments it keeps the full pool and the seeded randomness within each coverage tier.
outcome: dev 1.9725 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the current best pipeline exactly as it is (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter with _MIN_COVERAGE=0.6, _MIN_DF=20, _MIN_WORDS=5, seeded shuffle, no truncation) and add one extra survivor rule: drop any doc with fewer than 100 [A-Za-z]+ words (define _MIN_LONG_WORDS = 100 and apply it right after the coverage check, so `if len(ws) < _MIN_LONG_WORDS: continue`). Leave the vocabulary, the shuffle, and everything else unchanged.
why: Short fragments are the most likely to be noisy, boundary-heavy or off-domain residue, and the trainer only reads the first T tokens of a roughly 2T survivor list, so dropping short fragments should raise the share of coherent article-length text in what it actually trains on; this is an untested length criterion that does not repeat any rejected experiment.
outcome: dev 1.9530 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the current best pipeline exactly as it is (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter with _MIN_COVERAGE=0.6, _MIN_DF=20, _MIN_WORDS=5, seeded shuffle, no truncation). Add one new survivor rule, applied after the coverage check: drop any doc that matches an SEO/spam template regex, compiled once at module level as _SPAM_RE = re.compile(r"click here to order|discount code|\bcoupon\b|free shipping|order .{0,40} online, fast delivery|best price guaranteed|cheap .{0,30}! order", re.IGNORECASE). Use `if _SPAM_RE.search(docs[i]): continue`. Do not add an alphabetic-fraction rule, MinHash, target similarity, or any change to the vocabulary or the shuffle.
why: The vocabulary-coverage filter keeps spam docs because their words ("order", "online", "cheap", "free", "shipping") are frequent across the pool and so pass the df>=20 vocabulary test, and experiments 1–3 only tested spam phrases bundled with other changes that were rejected, so this isolated spam-template removal on top of the current best has not been measured.
outcome: dev 2.0017 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the current best pipeline unchanged (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter with _MIN_DF=20, _MIN_WORDS=5, seeded shuffle, no truncation) and lower the coverage threshold from _MIN_COVERAGE = 0.6 to _MIN_COVERAGE = 0.5. Change nothing else, and keep the fallback out of the way: the seeded shuffle of survivors is returned as before, cycled only if the total is below T.
why: Raising the threshold to 0.75 hurt (1.9568 vs 1.9470), which suggests the filter is already cutting useful text, so loosening it to 0.5 keeps more target-style documents while still removing the scrambled/junk docs that have low vocabulary coverage, and the 2T pool has enough slack that the extra tokens are not needed to fill T.
outcome: dev 1.9608 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In curate.py, change _MIN_DF from 20 to 50 and leave everything else as in the current best (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter with _MIN_COVERAGE=0.6, _MIN_WORDS=5, seeded shuffle, no truncation). The vocabulary is still target_sample words plus pool words with document frequency >= 50.
why: Spam templates and junk phrases repeat across many pool documents, so words like "cheap", "online" or "coupon" pass a df>=20 cutoff and make spam look covered; raising the cutoff to 50 keeps template-only words out of the vocabulary while common English words still pass, so damaged and spam docs should be dropped more reliably. This is untested, since _MIN_DF has never been varied in the experiments so far.
outcome: dev 1.9512 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the current best pipeline unchanged (exact dedupe, vocabulary-coverage filter with _MIN_COVERAGE=0.6, _MIN_DF=20, _MIN_WORDS=5, seeded shuffle, no truncation), and add a second dedupe pass after the exact dedupe: hash the first 200 characters of each stripped doc (after lowercasing and collapsing whitespace) and keep only the first occurrence of each prefix hash. Apply it to unique_idx before the vocabulary is built, so the DF counts also reflect the deduped pool. Leave everything else as it is.
why: The pool contains many templated documents (repeated nav bars, boilerplate headers, same-opening spam) that share a long common prefix but differ in the tail, so exact-hash dedupe misses them and they over-weight junk patterns; prefix dedupe removes that repetition cheaply without the spam-phrase or similarity rules that already failed.
outcome: dev 1.9562 against 1.9470 for the best at the time, rejected
